The companions pledged, like the women, not to associate anything with Allah, steal, commit adultery or kill; a punished sin is expiated, and one Allah conceals is left to Him.
No compensation is due for injury caused by an animal or by falling into a well or a mine, and a fifth is due on buried treasure.
The defendant must take the oath, for otherwise people would claim others' lives and property, and the Prophet also judged on an oath with a witness.
The Prophet said he judges disputes by what he hears, so whoever is given his brother's right by his ruling is given a portion of the Fire.
Hind told the Prophet her husband Abu Sufyan was miserly, and he allowed her to take from his wealth what was reasonable and sufficient for herself and her children.

Allah likes worship without partners and holding fast to His rope, forbids disobeying mothers, burying daughters alive and withholding rights, and dislikes idle talk, persistent questioning and wasting wealth.
A judge who strives and is right has two rewards and one who strives and errs has one, and no one should judge between two people while angry.
Innovating in the Prophet's affairs without valid reason, or doing any act without his sanction, is to be rejected.
The best witness is the one who gives his evidence before he is asked for it.
When a wolf took one of two women's sons, David judged for the elder, but Solomon, calling for a knife to divide the child, judged for the younger, who refused.
Buyer and seller of land both refused gold found in it, so their judge married one's son to the other's daughter and told them to spend and give charity.
Found property is announced for a year, its bag and strap noted, then used and repaid if the owner comes; a stray sheep may be taken, a camel left alone.
No one may milk another's animal without his permission, for its udders are its owner's store of food, as a storeroom no one would want broken into.
Guests are owed a day and night of special kindness and three days' hospitality, beyond that charity, must not exhaust their host, and may take their due when refused.
On a journey the Prophet told those with a spare mount or surplus provisions to give them to those without, and named many other kinds of wealth likewise.
Pooled on a small sheet at the Prophet's command, scarce expedition provisions fed fourteen hundred people, who filled their bags, and a small bucket of water sufficed their ablution.
Inviting the enemy to Islam was needed early on, and Banu Mustaliq were raided unawares; commanders were to offer Islam, emigration or jizya before fighting, never mutilating or killing children.
Sending companions on missions, including Mu'adh to Yemen, the Prophet told them to give glad tidings, be lenient and not harsh, and not create aversion.
On the Day of Judgment every perfidious person will have a flag proclaiming his treachery, raised in proportion to it, and no treachery is greater than that of a ruler.
War is a stratagem; do not wish to meet the enemy but ask Allah for safety, and when you meet them be firm: Paradise is under the shadows of swords.
The Prophet asked Allah, Revealer of the Book, to rout and shake the tribes, and at Uhud said if Allah willed, none would be left on earth to worship Him.
Finding a woman killed in battle, the Prophet forbade killing women and children; asked about polytheists' women and children struck in night raids, he said they are from them.
The Prophet had the date-palms of Banu Nadir at Buwaira cut down and burnt, and a verse came saying that trees cut or left standing were by Allah's permission.
An earlier prophet's spoils were consumed by fire once misappropriated gold was returned, spoils being lawful only for this community; Sa'd's request for a sword brought the verse on spoils.
Troops sent to Najd got twelve camels each and one extra; the Prophet gave small detachments more than a share in a large force, the fifth always being reserved.
The Prophet gave an enemy's belongings to his killer, as to Abu Qatada, one of Abu Jahl's slayers and Salama, but backed Khalid against a claim after Auf taunted him.
Abu Bakr gave Salama a captive girl taken from Fazara, and the Prophet asked him for her and sent her to Mecca as ransom for Muslims held prisoner there.
A township gained without war gives its takers a share, a fighting one a fifth to Allah and His Messenger; Banu Nadir's property, gained without fighting, was the Prophet's own.
Prophets leave no heirs, their legacy being charity, so Abu Bakr refused Fatima her share and Umar held Abbas and Ali to it; Ali later pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr.
The Prophet said his heirs would not share even a dinar of what he left: after his wives' maintenance and his manager's pay, all he leaves is charity.
The Prophet gave a horseman two shares of the spoils and a footman one.
At Badr Allah answers the Prophet's prayer with angels; he takes ransom for captives on Abu Bakr's advice, weeps at the punishment shown for it, and booty is made lawful.
Thumama b. Uthal, a captured chief of Yamama, is held bound in the mosque, questioned thrice, then freed by the Prophet; he bathes, embraces Islam and goes on to Umrah.
The Prophet calls the Jews to Islam, warning of expulsion; Banu Nadir are expelled, Quraiza's men killed after they fought, and he vows to expel Jews and Christians from Arabia.
Banu Quraiza surrender to Sa'd b. Mu'adh's judgment that their fighters be killed and families captured; Sa'd dies when his wound reopens, and companions differ over praying before reaching Quraiza.
The Ansar shared their orchards with the penniless Muhajirs, who returned these gifts after later conquests; the Prophet gave Umm Aiman, who had nursed him, other palms for those returned.
On the day of Khaibar Abdullah b. Mughaffal seized a bag of fat, vowing to give none of it away, then turned to find the Prophet smiling and felt ashamed.
Heraclius questions Abu Sufyan about the Prophet, then reads his letter inviting him to Islam; the Prophet also wrote inviting Chosroes, the Negus and every other ruler to Allah.
At Hunain the Muslims fall back before archers while the Prophet holds firm on his white mule; Abbas calls them back, and he throws pebbles at the enemy, who flee.
The Prophet besieges Ta'if without taking it; his companions resist leaving, a morning raid leaves them wounded, and they gladly depart the next day as he laughs.
